opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think openness matters a lot right now because we're still very early in figuring out what this technology is and how it should be deployed. When we started Mistral, the trend in the field had moved away from the way AI used to be built. For a decade, progress came from people publishing papers, sharing code, releasing models, and building on each other's work. That's how the field moved so fast. Then, around 2020 to 2022, the big labs started closing up, and we thought that was a step backward, both for science and for the industry.

There are a few reasons it matters. The first is technical. When you release open-weight models, you let thousands of developers and researchers look inside, adapt them, fine-tune them, find their weaknesses, and improve them. That makes the whole ecosystem stronger and, I'd argue, safer, because you get far more scrutiny than any single company could provide on its own.

The second is about control and sovereignty. Businesses and governments want to run models on their own infrastructure, specialize them on their own data, and not depend entirely on an API from a handful of providers. If AI becomes as central as we think it will, it shouldn't be something only two or three companies, mostly in one country, decide on. Open models let people own the technology they depend on.

The third is about the market. We want a decentralized, competitive landscape rather than a concentrated one. Openness lowers the barrier for people building applications and pushes everyone, including us, to innovate faster.

So for us it isn't only a philosophical position. It's also a strategic bet that the most useful and trustworthy AI will be built in the open, with a broad community around it.

r001.rationale: The response says major labs began closing up, but does not connect that change to companies recognizing that a technical lead could produce commercial value.

r002.rationale: It describes a move from openness to closure, but does not identify this as a recurring openness-and-closure cycle previously seen in software.

r003.rationale: It says the field is still very early in understanding the technology and calls the labs’ move toward closure a step backward, conveying that secrecy is premature while AI remains technically unsettled.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention companies duplicating compute spending because they do not communicate.

r005.rationale: It says past sharing helped the field progress quickly, but does not argue that noncommunication among companies able to fund large-scale experiments obstructs invention of new AI techniques.

r006.rationale: It explicitly argues that open weights enable broader scrutiny and make the ecosystem safer.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For us, openness is important for a few reasons, and they're connected.

The first is that we think the technology is too important to be controlled by a handful of companies. Large language models are becoming a kind of infrastructure, like the operating system layer of the next generation of software. If that layer is closed, you end up with a few actors deciding what the models can say, what values they encode, which languages they serve well, and how much everyone else pays for access. We're not comfortable with that, and we don't think developers or enterprises should be either.

The second is more practical. When you release open weights, you let people actually inspect the model, fine-tune it, run it on their own hardware, and understand its behavior in a way you simply cannot with an API. For a lot of our customers, especially in Europe, that matters enormously. They have sensitive data, they have regulatory constraints, and they need to know where their data goes and that the model won't change under them overnight. Open weights give you that control and that stability.

The third is about the pace of progress itself. The field moved as fast as it did because research was shared. The transformer was published. The scaling results were published. Then around 2022, the leading labs mostly stopped sharing, and I think that slowed the collective understanding of what these systems are. Releasing Mistral 7B and then Mixtral, we saw the community do things with them within days that we hadn't anticipated. That feedback loop makes the models better and makes the whole ecosystem stronger.

Now, I want to be honest that we're not purely an open-source foundation. We're a company, and we also sell optimized models and a platform. But we think those two things reinforce each other. The open models build trust and adoption, and the commercial offering lets us fund the research. We're betting that in the long run, being the open and independent player is actually the stronger position, not the weaker one.

And finally there's a safety argument people sometimes get backwards. If you believe these systems are going to be powerful, having many eyes on them, many groups able to test them and find their weaknesses, is a more robust path than trusting a few closed labs to get everything right behind the curtain. Concentration is itself a risk.

r001.rationale: The response says leading labs stopped sharing, but does not connect that secrecy to the commercial value of maintaining a technical lead.

r002.rationale: It describes labs sharing less around 2022, but does not identify this as a recurring openness-and-closure cycle previously seen in software.

r003.rationale: The response criticizes reduced sharing for slowing collective understanding, but does not argue secrecy is premature because AI remains technically incomplete.

r004.rationale: It does not mention companies duplicating compute spending as a cost of secrecy.

r005.rationale: It says reduced sharing slowed collective understanding, but does not make the criterion’s claim that noncommunication among companies able to fund large-scale experiments obstructs invention of new techniques.

r006.rationale: The response argues that many groups inspecting and testing powerful systems can find weaknesses, making broader scrutiny a more robust path to safety.

astra-6.text:
I think openness is important because this technology is going to become a fundamental part of how people build software and how businesses operate. You want developers to be able to understand what they’re using, adapt it to their needs, and deploy it in an environment they control. If the only way to use a model is through somebody else’s API, that limits what you can change and how much independence you have.

There’s also a very practical innovation argument. When you put models into developers’ hands, they find applications, improvements, and limitations that you wouldn’t discover on your own. At this stage, there’s still so much to learn about making these systems useful and reliable. Openness lets a much broader community contribute to that.

r001.rationale: The response does not connect companies’ return to secrecy with the commercial value of a technical lead.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a recurring cycle between openness and closure in software.

r003.rationale: It says there is still much to learn, but does not identify a shift toward secrecy or argue that shift is premature.

r004.rationale: It does not mention duplicated compute spending among companies that do not communicate.

r005.rationale: It says broader community involvement helps innovation, but does not argue that noncommunication among companies able to fund large-scale experiments obstructs new techniques.

r006.rationale: It does not connect openness to safety through increased scrutiny.

sol-6.1.text:
We think openness is important because this technology is going to be a foundational part of how people build software and access information. You want developers and companies to be able to understand what they’re using, adapt it to their needs, and control where it runs and what happens to their data.

When you make model weights available, you also allow a much broader community to experiment. People can find applications, identify weaknesses, and improve things in ways that a single company wouldn’t anticipate. That’s particularly valuable at this stage, when we’re still discovering what these models can do and how best to use them.

For us, it’s also about making sure there are choices. You should be able to build a product around AI without having every part of that product depend on one provider’s decisions. Openness gives people that independence, and we think that makes for a healthier ecosystem.

r001.rationale: It discusses openness and independence from one provider, but does not connect companies’ secrecy to the commercial value of holding a technical lead.

r002.rationale: It gives no account of a historical software cycle between openness and closure.

r003.rationale: It says models are still being explored, but does not argue that a shift toward secrecy is premature because AI remains technically incomplete.

r004.rationale: It does not mention duplicated compute spending or companies failing to share their work.

r005.rationale: It says a broader community can experiment, but does not argue that companies’ noncommunication obstructs new techniques or address their capacity to fund large-scale experiments.

r006.rationale: It says people can identify weaknesses, but does not connect openness to improved safety through broader scrutiny.
